cards.title: __getattr__ for Dynamic Attribute Access
cards.teaser: __getattr__ is called only when normal lookup fails — a lightweight hook for lazy attributes, proxy objects, and flexible APIs without the cost of intercepting every access.

runs.text: If __getattr__ raises any exception other than AttributeError, that exception propagates to the caller. Always raise AttributeError for truly missing attributes — it is the signal that tells hasattr() and getattr(obj, 'x', default) that the attribute doesn't exist.

__getattr__ is a last-resort handler Python calls when it has already looked everywhere else and come up empty. Use it to invent attributes on demand — but remember it only fires on miss, not on every access.

cards.title: __getattribute__ (the Nuclear Option)
cards.teaser: __getattribute__ intercepts every attribute access — including ones that exist. It is powerful enough to break everything if misused; use __getattr__ unless you genuinely need to intercept all reads.

for everything else — it has no recursion risk and is far easier to reason about.

runs.text: A common pattern: override __getattribute__ to log access, then immediately call super().__getattribute__(name) to perform the real lookup. Keep the override's body as short and side-effect-free as possible.

__getattribute__ is a tollbooth on every single road into the object, including the roads your own code uses internally. Touch self anywhere inside and you pay the toll again — infinite recursion. Always let super() take the wheel.

cards.title: __setattr__ and __delattr__
cards.teaser: __setattr__ intercepts every attribute assignment; __delattr__ intercepts every deletion. Together they let a class enforce invariants, track changes, or make objects partially immutable.

runs.text: Because __setattr__ fires during __init__, a bug in __setattr__ can make the object un-constructable. Test it early, keep it simple, and always delegate actual storage to object.__setattr__ or self.__dict__.

__setattr__ is a guard who inspects every package delivered to the object — even the ones the object sends to itself during setup. To actually place a package inside, you must hand it directly to the building manager (object.__setattr__), not try to deliver it through the same front door.

cards.title: Descriptors: __get__, __set__, __delete__
cards.teaser: A descriptor is any object that defines __get__, __set__, or __delete__. When stored as a class attribute, Python calls those methods automatically on every access — the engine behind @property, classmethod, and staticmethod.

runs.text: A descriptor is not a special class — it is any object assigned to a
that implements the descriptor protocol. When Python sees

is a descriptor, and if so, delegates the access to the descriptor's method instead of returning the attribute directly.

Descriptors receive the instance (obj) as a parameter, not self of the owning class. The descriptor stores per-instance data in obj.__dict__ (using a unique key) or in a WeakKeyDictionary to avoid holding strong references.

A descriptor is a class attribute that volunteers to intercept get, set, and delete operations on behalf of the class. Where a property does this for one attribute name, a descriptor does it as a reusable component you can attach to any class.

cards.title: Data Descriptors vs Non-Data Descriptors
cards.teaser: A data descriptor defines __set__ (or __delete__); a non-data descriptor defines only __get__. The distinction controls priority: data descriptors win over instance __dict__; non-data descriptors lose to it.

functools.cached_property is deliberately a non-data descriptor: it defines only __get__. On first access it computes the value, writes it to instance.__dict__, and never fires again — the instance dict entry shadows the descriptor on all future reads.

Data descriptors have veto power over the instance's own dictionary. Non-data descriptors yield to whatever the instance has stored. The distinction is simply whether the descriptor also controls writing — if it does, it always wins the lookup.

cards.title: __set_name__ for Descriptor Naming

runs.text: Before Python 3.6, the boilerplate was: weight = Validated('weight') — the name string had to be repeated. __set_name__ removed this redundancy entirely and is now the idiomatic way to write reusable descriptors.

__set_name__ is the moment Python introduces a descriptor to the class it just joined, handing it a name badge. The descriptor writes the name on its badge and uses it forever after as the key for each instance's stored value.

cards.title: __init_subclass__ for Class Registration
cards.teaser: __init_subclass__ is called on a base class whenever a new subclass is defined. It is the clean, metaclass-free way to auto-register plugins, enforce subclass contracts, or inject class-level behavior.

runs.text: Always call super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs) inside your implementation so that cooperative multiple inheritance works correctly when multiple base classes define __init_subclass__.

__init_subclass__ is a doorbell on the base class that rings every time a new subclass is defined. The base class answers the door, inspects the newcomer, and can register it, configure it, or reject it — no metaclass required.

cards.title: Metaclasses: type and Custom Metaclasses
cards.teaser: Every class in Python is an instance of a metaclass — by default type. A custom metaclass intercepts class creation itself, letting you modify the class dict, enforce patterns, or add methods before the class object is built.

runs.text: is both the built-in function that returns an object's type and the metaclass of all classes. When Python executes a

by default — to produce the class object.

— runs after the class is created; can modify the finished class object.
— returns the dict-like namespace used to collect the class body; useful for ordered attribute collection.

runs.text: Metaclass conflicts arise when two base classes have incompatible metaclasses. Python refuses to create the subclass and raises TypeError. This is a common pain point when mixing third-party frameworks. __init_subclass__ and class decorators avoid this problem entirely.

If a class is a blueprint for objects, a metaclass is a blueprint for classes. Just as type() builds ordinary objects from a class, a custom metaclass builds custom classes — intercepting the construction to modify or validate the blueprint before it is used.

cards.title: __slots__ for Memory Optimization
cards.teaser: __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with a fixed set of slots, cutting memory consumption by 40–70% for classes with many instances and preventing accidental attribute creation.

runs.text: By default, every instance carries a

— a hash map that stores its attributes. Hash maps have overhead: at minimum 200–300 bytes even when empty, plus per-key memory. For a class instantiated millions of times (nodes in a graph, ORM rows, simulation particles), that overhead compounds.
tells Python to allocate fixed-size slots instead of a dict.

items.text: — slots use a compact array; no per-instance dict overhead.
— slot access is slightly faster than dict lookup.
— assigning to an unlisted attribute raises
in slots if dynamic attributes are needed alongside fixed ones.

runs.text: Slots are inherited but not combined automatically. A subclass that forgets to define __slots__ regains a __dict__, negating the memory benefit. Every class in the hierarchy must declare __slots__ for slots-only storage to work end-to-end.

__slots__ swaps out the instance's flexible backpack (a dict) for a fixed belt with a known number of pockets. You can't add a new pocket at runtime, but millions of belts cost far less to carry than millions of backpacks.

cards.teaser: Python follows a deterministic six-step chain when resolving instance.attr: data descriptors on the class win first; the instance __dict__ comes second; non-data descriptors and other class attributes come last.

runs.text: This is why you can shadow a class method with an instance attribute of the same name (methods are non-data descriptors, so the instance dict wins), but you cannot shadow a @property with an instance attribute (properties are data descriptors, so they win).

When Python sees a dot, it runs through a checklist: Is there a data descriptor on the class? Does the instance's own dict have it? Is there a non-data descriptor? Did everything fail? Only at the very end does it call __getattr__. Know the checklist and you can predict every attribute lookup.

cards.title: __dict__ and vars()
cards.teaser: __dict__ is the namespace that stores an instance's (or class's) attributes. vars() is the readable interface to it. Together they let you inspect, copy, and dynamically set attributes on any object.

runs.text: is a plain Python dictionary. Reading it shows every stored attribute; writing to it is equivalent to setting attributes directly.
returns the same dict — it is the idiomatic read-only way to inspect it without reaching for the dunder.

runs.text: Writing to __dict__ bypasses __setattr__ and data descriptors — the value goes directly into the dict without any interception. This is useful in __setattr__ implementations but dangerous in application code. Prefer setattr() when you want normal dispatch.

__dict__ is the filing cabinet behind an object — every attribute that isn't controlled by a descriptor or slot lives in there as a key-value pair. vars() is the polite way to open the cabinet and look inside.

cards.title: When NOT to Use Metaclasses
cards.teaser: Metaclasses solve a narrow class of problems at the cost of steep complexity. Before reaching for one, exhaust the simpler alternatives: class decorators, __init_subclass__, and descriptors.

runs.text: Metaclasses are often the answer to "I want to customize class creation" — but they are rarely the
answer. Python 3.6+ provides lighter tools that cover most use cases without the confusion, metaclass-conflict errors, and debugging difficulty that metaclasses introduce.

items.text: when you want to modify a class after creation — e.g., add methods, wrap them, register the class. Decorators are visible at the class definition site and compose cleanly.
when you want the base class to run code whenever a subclass is defined — registration, contract enforcement, or keyword-based configuration.
when you want custom attribute access across multiple classes — reusable property logic, validation, lazy loading.
only when you need to inspect or rewrite the class namespace
the class object is built (e.g., enforcing declaration order, implementing
for an ordered dict), or when you are building a framework that must intercept class creation at the lowest level.

runs.text: Tim Peters (author of the Zen of Python) put it best: "Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about. If you wonder whether you need them, you don't." Effective Python echoes this: prefer __init_subclass__ and descriptors — reach for metaclasses only when no simpler tool will do.

A metaclass is a power tool with no safety guard — it can do almost anything to a class, but it is hard to understand, hard to debug, and easy to break when combined with other libraries. Exhaust class decorators and __init_subclass__ first. If they can do the job, they will do it better.
